title: Memory and addresses
lesson:
In Level 1 you wrote `void addDamage(int& health, int dmg)` so a function could change the caller's variable. That `&` was your first look at **memory**. Level 2 is about how C++ stores things, who owns them, and how to clean up. This is the part of C++ that Python and C# hide from you, and the part Unreal expects you to understand.

**Stack and heap, in plain words.** Every variable lives somewhere in memory, and every place in memory has an **address** (a number, like a house number).

- The **stack** holds a function's local variables. They appear when the function starts and vanish when it ends. Fast, automatic, tidy.
- The **heap** is a big shared space for things that must live longer, or whose size you only know while running (a level's enemies, a loaded texture). You ask for heap memory and something must give it back. Units 3 to 6 are about that.

**Addresses and pointers.** `&x` gives the address of `x`. A **pointer** is a variable that holds an address. `*p` follows the pointer to the thing it points at.

```
int ammo = 30;
int* p = &ammo;   // p holds ammo's address
*p = 25;          // follow p and change what's there: ammo is now 25
std::cout << p;   // some address like 0x61fe14
```

**nullptr** means "points at nothing". Following a null pointer (`*p` when `p` is `nullptr`) crashes the program, so check first: `if (p) ...` or `if (p != nullptr) ...`. That habit saves hours.

**References vs pointers.** Both let you reach someone else's variable.

- A **reference** (`int& h`) is another name for one variable. It can't be null and can't be re-pointed. Use it for "this function works on your thing".
- A **pointer** (`int* p`) can be `nullptr` and can be moved to point somewhere else. Use it for "maybe there is a thing" (a turret's current target, which may be none) or when you will point at different things over time.

```
void heal(int& hp)        { hp += 10; }          // there is always an hp
void healTarget(int* hp)  { if (hp) *hp += 10; } // there may be no target
```

**The common mistake:** keeping a pointer to something that has gone away, like a pointer to a local variable after its function returned, or to a vector item after the vector grew and moved. The pointer still holds the old address, but nothing valid lives there. It is called a **dangling pointer**, and it is the most famous bug in C++.

In Unreal you will see pointers everywhere: `AActor* Target`, `UStaticMeshComponent* Mesh`. Almost every one can be null, which is why Unreal code is full of `if (Target)` checks.

notes: int* p = &ammo; stores ammo's address in p; *p = 25 changes ammo through it.
target->hp is short for (*target).hp: follow the pointer, then take the field.
heal takes a reference because there is always an hp to change.
hitTarget takes a pointer because there may be no target, and it checks for nullptr before using it.

exercises.title: Swap through pointers
exercises.prompt: Write void swapPtr(int* a, int* b) that swaps the two ints a and b point at. If either pointer is nullptr, do nothing.

tests.call: []{ int a = 1, b = 2; swapPtr(&a, &b); return a * 10 + b; }()
[]{ int a = 4, b = 9; swapPtr(&b, &a); return a * 10 + b; }()
[]{ int a = 5; swapPtr(&a, nullptr); return a; }()
tests.hint_if_fail: Check both pointers before following them.

hints: *a is the int that a points at. You need a temporary int to hold one value.

exercises.title: Ammo by reference and by pointer
exercises.prompt:
Write two functions that add n rounds of ammo, never going above 99.
void addAmmoRef(int& ammo, int n) works on a reference.
bool addAmmoPtr(int* ammo, int n) works on a pointer: if ammo is nullptr it returns false and does nothing, otherwise it adds and returns true.

tests.call: []{ int a = 10; bool ok = addAmmoPtr(&a, 5); return ok ? a : -1; }()

hints: The reference version uses ammo like a normal int. The pointer version uses *ammo.
if (!ammo) return false; *ammo += n; if (*ammo > 99) *ammo = 99; return true;

exercises.title: Lock on to a target
exercises.prompt:
Enemy is given. Write Enemy* lockOn(std::vector<Enemy>& enemies, const std::string& name): a pointer to the first enemy with that name, or nullptr if there is none.
Then write bool shoot(Enemy* target, int dmg): if target is nullptr return false; otherwise lower its hp by dmg (never below 0) and return true.

tests.call: []{ std::vector<Enemy> es = {{"Goblin", 30}, {"Orc", 50}}; Enemy* t = lockOn(es, "Orc"); return t ? t->hp : -1; }()

tests.hint_if_fail: Return the address of the item inside the vector (&e), not a copy.

tests.call: []{ Enemy e{"Rat", 5}; bool ok = shoot(&e, 20); return ok ? e.hp : -1; }()
[]{ std::vector<Enemy> es = {{"Bat", 1}, {"Bat", 2}}; Enemy* t = lockOn(es, "Bat"); return t ? t->hp : -1; }()

hints: Loop with for (Enemy& e : enemies). The & matters: without it e is a copy that dies at the end of the loop.
shoot: if (!target) return false; target->hp -= dmg; if (target->hp < 0) target->hp = 0; return true;

quiz.q: int x = 5; int* p = &x; *p = 8; What is x now?
quiz.why: *p is x itself, so writing to *p changes x.

quiz.q: A turret may have no current target. Which parameter type fits best?
quiz.why: A pointer can be null, which says 'maybe there is no target'.

quiz.q: What happens if you do *p when p is nullptr?
quiz.why: There is nothing at a null pointer to read.

quiz.q: Where do a function's local variables live?
choices: On the stack, and they vanish when the function returns
quiz.why: The stack is automatic: in when the function starts, out when it ends.

quiz.q: A function returns &local where local is its own int. What is the result?
choices: A dangling pointer to memory that is no longer valid
quiz.why: local died when the function returned; the address now points at nothing valid.

cards.q: Follow pointer p to its value?

cards.a: nullptr. Check with if (p) before using it.
Reference when there is always a thing; pointer when there might be none or it changes.

explain: Explain the difference between a reference and a pointer in your own words, with a game example where each one is the right choice.
